about: Facts for the five shark species in the SharkCam Mumbai running example. The facts come from FishBase, GBIF's copy of IUCN Red List categories, and peer-reviewed studies of Indian landings. The catch records built from these facts are made up (see catch.json). Fields marked verified:false were not confirmed in a source we opened.

units.length: total length (TL) in cm unless stated
units.weight: grams in the length-weight law W = a * L^b, with L in cm TL
units.maturity: L50 is the total length (cm) at which half of the animals are mature

local_names.source: FishBase common names table (Latin-script entries cite Venkateswarlu 1984; Devanagari entries give no reference). Names vary by port. Not checked with a native speaker.

species.max_length_note: FishBase lists 100 cm TL (sizes up to 120 cm unconfirmed). The IUCN account says to 91 cm TL. The largest animal in the 2016 to 2017 Mumbai landing sample was 61 cm.
species.landing_length_source: Gladston et al. (2018), mixed sexes, n = 543, samples from Sassoon Dock, Versova, New Ferry Wharf, Satpati and Naigaon landings, Aug 2016 to Oct 2017. Mean length in the catch was 40.5 cm in a Gujarat sample (Dash et al. (2018)).

length_weight.units: W in grams, L = total length in cm
length_weight.source: Gladston et al. (2018), Journal of Applied Ichthyology 34(3):753-757, doi:10.1111/jai.13680 (north-eastern Arabian Sea, 18 to 61 cm TL). Values read from the FishBase length-weight table (FishBase reference 121648); the paper's full text was not open to us.
length_weight.cross_check: Malvan, Maharashtra: a = 0.00382, b = 2.97 (Eswaran et al. (2023), 16.8 to 58.7 cm TL, n = 304).

species.l50_source: Dash et al. (2018), Journal of Applied Ichthyology 34:1304-1313, doi:10.1111/jai.13794 (Gujarat coast, 1,277 sharks). The abstract gives 33.8 cm for males and 35.8 cm for females as lengths at maturity. The pooled value 35 cm is the mean of the two, rounded.
species.l50_other_estimates: FishBase lists Lm = 38.3 cm (range 33 to 76.5 cm). Malvan males: L50 = 41.3 cm (Eswaran et al. (2023)).

iucn.account: Dulvy et al. (2021), The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2021
iucn.how_checked: Category confirmed with the GBIF API; assessment date and criteria from FishBase (Red List version 2025-2); account text read in the CMFRI repository. The iucnredlist.org site blocks scripted access, so its page was not opened.

species.habitat: Coastal and estuarine waters, mostly over muddy and sandy bottoms (IUCN) and also reported on rocky ground (FishBase), often near large freshwater outflows. Lives near the sea floor and forms large schools.
species.depth_note: IUCN account: 10 to 75 m, more typically less than 50 m. FishBase lists 10 to 13 m from a single record.
species.plain_fact: The spadenose shark is the shark most often brought ashore in Pakistan, northern India and Bangladesh. It is under a metre long, matures at about two years and has litters of 6 to 20 pups.

sources.label: IUCN account (Dulvy et al. (2021)) in the CMFRI repository

species.notes: Taxonomy of Scoliodon is under revision, so older Indian studies may mix more than one species. The L50 values are from Gujarat, the next state north of Maharashtra, because no Mumbai study with a full text was found. FishBase lists a Mumbai value of 35 cm for females (2014) without a method.

local_names.source: FishBase common names table (Latin-script entries cite Venkateswarlu 1984; Devanagari entries give no reference). Names vary by port. Not checked with a native speaker.

species.max_length_note: FishBase lists 175 cm TL (male or unsexed). Animals measured in Indian landings are far smaller: the largest in the Mumbai landing sample was 97 cm. Treat 175 cm as an upper bound from the global literature.
species.landing_length_source: Gladston et al. (2018), mixed sexes, n = 95, Maharashtra landings including Sassoon Dock.

length_weight.units: W in grams, L = total length in cm
length_weight.source: Gladston et al. (2018), Journal of Applied Ichthyology 34(3):753-757, doi:10.1111/jai.13680 (north-eastern Arabian Sea, 55 to 97 cm TL). Values read from the FishBase length-weight table (FishBase reference 121648).
length_weight.cross_check: Karnataka, India: a = 0.0020, b = 3.142 for females (FishBase table, 32.6 to 144 cm TL).

species.l50_source: Dash et al. (2018), Ichthyological Research 65:324-333, doi:10.1007/s10228-018-0627-6 (Gujarat coast, 684 sharks). The abstract gives 61.5 cm for males and 61.3 cm for females. The pooled value is the mean of the two.
species.l50_other_estimates: FishBase lists 75 cm from South Africa and Indonesia, and 70 to 82.5 cm from West Africa.

iucn.how_checked: Category confirmed with the GBIF API; assessment date and criteria from FishBase (Red List version 2025-2). The iucnredlist.org site blocks scripted access, so its page was not opened.

species.habitat: Continental shelf waters, often off sandy beaches, rarely in estuaries. It feeds mainly on small fishes and cephalopods and sometimes enters fresh water.
species.depth_note: FishBase: 1 to 200 m. FishBase also says it occurs near the surface in shallow water.
species.plain_fact: Milk sharks sometimes swim into fresh water. FishBase records them in Cambodia as far upstream as the Great Lake.
species.notes: Genetic work suggests the milk shark may be a complex of several species, so values from other oceans may not match Indian animals. The L50 values are from Gujarat.

local_names.source: FishBase common names table. Names vary by port. Not checked with a native speaker.

species.max_length_note: FishBase, male or unsexed, total length.
species.landing_length_source: Eswaran et al. (2023), Malvan (south of Mumbai on the Maharashtra coast), 32.0 to 62.6 cm TL, n = 53. No Mumbai landing study of this species was found.

length_weight.units: W in grams, L = total length in cm
length_weight.source: Eswaran et al. (2023), Journal of the Marine Biological Association of India 65(2):62-67, doi:10.6024/jmbai.2023.65.2.2433-09, Table 1 (Malvan, Maharashtra). Units are not written in the abstract; the table's weights of 100 to 862 g for lengths of 32 to 62.6 cm confirm cm and grams.
length_weight.cross_check: Devadoss 1987 (Indian Journal of Fisheries 34(3):343-347) gives log10 W = -4.8378 + 2.7314 log10 L, which Eswaran et al. write as W = 0.00001453 L^2.7314. That form fits L in mm and W in g, which converts to a = 0.0078 for L in cm. FishBase lists a = 0.0145 and b = 2.731 for the same study, a factor of 1.9 higher. We could not resolve the difference.

species.l50_source: Devadoss 1987, Indian Journal of Fisheries 34(3):343-347 (specimens from both coasts of India). The abstract says males mature at 520 mm and females at 530 mm total length. The pooled value is the mean of the two.
species.l50_other_estimates: Eswaran et al. (2023) could not fit a maturity curve for this species because few mature animals were sampled (28 males, 12 females). For the related Arabian carpetshark (C. arabicum) they found L50 = 57.2 cm for males and 58.3 cm for females.

iucn.how_checked: Category confirmed with the GBIF API; assessment date and criteria from FishBase (Red List version 2025-2). The iucnredlist.org site blocks scripted access, so its page was not opened.

species.habitat: A common inshore bottom shark, often found in estuaries and near reefs. It probably feeds mainly on invertebrates and lays eggs in small oval egg cases on the sea floor.
species.plain_fact: A young grey bamboo shark has 12 or 13 dark bands across its back. The bands fade as it grows and adults have none, so a juvenile and an adult look quite different.
species.notes: Bamboo sharks are mixed up easily: the Arabian carpetshark (C. arabicum) lives in the same waters. The maturity lengths come from an abstract of a 1987 paper whose full text was not open to us. In the catch table, many bamboo sharks are logged on dives and in shallow pools rather than at the landing. That is a story choice for the primer, not a literature finding.

local_names.source: FishBase common names table (Latin-script entries cite Venkateswarlu 1984; Devanagari entries give no reference). Names vary by port. Not checked with a native speaker.

species.max_length_note: FishBase, male or unsexed, total length. Indian landings are mostly juveniles under 100 cm.
species.landing_length_source: Thomas et al. (2021), India-wide landings 2007 to 2018. The usual size class was 30 to 100 cm, and 79.5% of males and 83.2% of females measured 40 to 100 cm.

length_weight.units: W in grams, L = total length in cm (units assumed; see cross_check)
length_weight.applies_to: females (the male law is in by_sex)
length_weight.source: Thomas et al. (2021), Aquatic Conservation 31(11):3072-3086, doi:10.1002/aqc.3686, from the abstract: W = 0.0131 L^2.769 for females and W = 0.0218 L^2.634 for males (Indian waters).
length_weight.cross_check: The abstract does not state units. Both laws give about 4.0 to 4.5 kg at 100 cm, which matches the CMFRI Karnataka law (a = 0.00353, b = 3.07, about 4.9 kg at 100 cm; CMFRI annual report 2016-17, via FishBase).

species.l50_source: Thomas et al. (2021), doi:10.1002/aqc.3686 (abstract): about 168 cm TL for males and 239.6 cm TL for females. The pooled value 204 cm is the mean of the two, rounded, and is not a published figure.
species.l50_other_estimates: FishBase lists Indian values of 164 cm for males and 225 cm for females (Karnataka), and 152.5 cm for females elsewhere in India. World estimates run from 140 to 250 cm.

iucn.how_checked: Category confirmed with the GBIF API; assessment date and criteria from FishBase (Red List version 2025-2). The iucnredlist.org site blocks scripted access, so its page was not opened.

species.habitat: A coastal and semi-oceanic shark that often comes close inshore and enters bays and estuaries. Landings in India are dominated by juveniles.
species.depth_note: FishBase: usually 0 to 25 m, found to about 275 m, and recorded to 1,043 m.
species.plain_fact: Most scalloped hammerheads brought ashore in India are young. About 8 in 10 measured between 40 and 100 cm, although the species can grow past 4 m.

sources.label: Thomas et al. (2021) (hammerhead fishery in Indian waters)
Thomas et al. (2021) in the CMFRI repository

species.notes: The hammerhead values come from an abstract (full text not open to us). Because the maturity sizes of males and females differ by more than 70 cm, the catch generator uses the sex-specific L50 values. Nearly all hammerheads in a landing table are immature.

local_names.source: FishBase common names table (Latin-script entries cite Venkateswarlu 1984). Names vary by region. Not checked with a native speaker.

species.max_length_note: FishBase lists 204 cm TL. The female recorded at Sassoon Docks in February 2016 measured 266 cm TL (Jabado et al. (2018)), which is larger than the FishBase maximum.
species.landing_length_source: Too few records exist. Newborns measure 56 to 61 cm (FishBase).

length_weight.units: W in grams, L = total length in cm
length_weight.applies_to: proxy: bull shark Carcharhinus leucas, females 72 to 109.8 cm TL
length_weight.source: No length-weight law exists for the Ganges shark in FishBase. The proxy is the bull shark (Carcharhinus leucas) relation from Vermilion Bay, USA, listed in the FishBase length-weight table for that species. FishBase notes that the Ganges shark was long confused with the bull shark.
length_weight.cross_check: Weights from this law at 150 cm are about 29 kg. No measured weights for the Ganges shark were found.

species.l50_source: Proxy only. Wikipedia gives an estimated 178 cm at maturity, citing Compagno (1984, 2005). FishBase has no maturity entry. We did not open Compagno's text.

iucn.how_checked: Category confirmed with the GBIF API; assessment date and criteria from FishBase (Red List version 2025-2). The iucnredlist.org site blocks scripted access, so its page was not opened.

species.habitat: Rivers, estuaries and inshore waters. Its tiny eyes suggest it lives in muddy water with poor visibility. Biology is poorly known.
species.depth_note: FishBase gives no depth range. The 2016 Mumbai animal was a landing at Sassoon Docks, so the capture depth is not known.
species.plain_fact: A 266 cm female seen at Sassoon Docks in Mumbai in February 2016 was the first record of the Ganges shark from anywhere in its range in more than ten years.

sources.label: FishBase length-weight table for the proxy, Carcharhinus leucas
Jabado et al. (2018), Journal of Fish Biology 92(5):1663-1669 (Sassoon Docks record)
Jabado et al. (2018) in the JCU repository
Wikipedia (estimated size at maturity; secondary source)

species.notes: Length-weight law and L50 are proxys from a close relative or a secondary source, and are marked verified:false. The catch table contains only 3 made-up Ganges shark records. They are not the 2016 specimen.
